source.text: וַֽ/יִּשְׁחֲט֖וּ אֶת הַ/פָּ֑ר וַ/יָּבִ֥יאוּ אֶת הַ/נַּ֖עַר אֶל עֵלִֽי־־־׃

translation.text: Then they slaughtered[a] the bull and brought the boy[b] to Eli[c].

footnotes.text: Or 'killed.' The Hebrew verb can be rendered more generally, but 'slaughtered' better reflects the sacrificial context.
Or 'the child.' Hebrew naʿar can refer to a boy, child, or young man depending on context.

The retained Masoretic account has plural verbs without naming the participants here. The selected Septuagint text gives a longer sequence involving the father's recurring sacrifice, bringing the boy forward, and slaughtering the bull; it names Hannah in the final presentation to Eli. These are differences in the narrative, not just alternative translations of the same Hebrew. See also the note on 1:24.

lexical_decisions.rationale: The retained WLC wayyiqtol is plural and advances the narrative; the participants are not named in this clause. 'Slaughtered' preserves the sacrificial context and 'Then' the sequential presentation. The selected Greek text has a longer sacrifice sequence and a singular slaughtering verb at this point. This disclosure does not establish which narrative is earlier or identify the unnamed Hebrew participants; no fresh HALOT consultation is claimed.

פַּר commonly denotes a bull, often in sacrificial settings. The WLC noun here is singular with the article, so 'the bull' is retained. The current POB/WLC verse 24 reads 'three bulls'; 'a three-year-old bull' belongs to an alternative textual form. The singular in verse 25 contributes to that textual question but does not alone settle it or justify silently pluralizing this verse.

The retained WLC wayyiqtol is plural, with no named subject here; 'and brought' coordinates with the preceding English plural subject. The selected Greek text names Hannah in the final presentation to Eli within a longer narrative. This is a textual difference, not permission to insert Hannah into the retained Hebrew rendering, and does not settle historical priority; no fresh HALOT consultation is claimed.
נַעַר covers a range from child to young man; in this context Samuel is still very young, so 'boy' best matches the narrative situation more precisely than the broader 'child.'
אֶל normally indicates movement toward a person or place. 'To Eli' is the straightforward rendering in readable modern English.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Render the verb as 'slaughtered' to preserve the likely sacrificial setting without adding explanatory wording not present in the Hebrew.
theological_decisions.rationale: The immediate context concerns worship and offerings at Shiloh. 'Slaughtered' preserves that cultic resonance while remaining a direct translation of the Hebrew verb.
